steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on sequence length learning in transformer encoder models for text classification: why using sequence length as a shortcut is a problem, and what we study and propose to mitigate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Transformers are strong but can learn classification shortcuts
- Known shortcuts: bias and spurious features
- Sequence length as a lesser-known shortcut and why it is harmful
- Our motivation: insurance claims
- Contributions
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Transformers are strong but can learn classification shortcuts
  - transformer-based models: go-to for state of the art, impressive in most NLP tasks
  - parameter-heavy, trained on huge corpora -> retain most training data information
  - improvements sometimes rely on unknown, undesirable correlations in train/test data
  - models leverage these correlations as classification shortcuts
- Known shortcuts: bias and spurious features
  - bias: e.g. model associates gender and occupation instead of learning useful text representations to infer occupation
  - shortcuts improve models during construction ("good for the wrong reasons") but cause problems along the value chain if end users don't know the heuristic
  - spurious features: inductive bias from artifacts of annotation process or text structure -> models learn the dataset, not the task
- Sequence length as a lesser-known shortcut
  - sequence length difference between observations of different classes
  - any length variation, regardless of content, can cause misclassifications
  - hurts explanation mechanisms (main features not textual content)
  - artificial overperformance on train and test sets -> unfair comparisons for model selection; some models converge to local minimum using length
  - to avoid: gain comes at expense of robustness, explainability, evaluation
- Motivation
  - seldom seen in public/open datasets
  - our work: early warnings of catastrophic (costly) claims for analysts
  - basic vs catastrophic claim files have different length profiles
- Contributions
  - empirical study of how transformer-based models are affected by sequence length learning
  - evaluation of techniques using pretrained transformer capabilities to mitigate it
- Organization
  - Section 2: literature on identifying/addressing the problem
  - Section 3: experiments on impact of sequence length meta-feature, four text classification datasets
  - Section 4: data-centric mitigation techniques

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based models are the current go-to models for state-of-the-art performance, and they get impressive performances in most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. These models have a lot of parameters and are trained on huge corpora, so they retain most of the information in the training data, and this leads to significant improvements. But sometimes these improvements rely on correlations in the training and test data that are unknown and undesirable. Models can learn to use these correlations as classification shortcuts.

Bias is a well-known source of shortcuts. For example, a model that uses bias as a shortcut could associate gender and occupation together instead of learning useful textual representations that would help it infer the occupation of someone. Using shortcuts can make the model better during construction, since the models are good for the wrong reasons, but it can create problems along the value chain when the end users do not know what heuristic is used. Spurious features are another source of classification shortcuts. In this case the inductive model bias is generated by artifacts from the annotation process or from the text structure, so the models learn the dataset and not the task.

A shortcut that is less known is the difference in sequence length between observations of different classes in a classification task. If a model exploits this feature, then any variation in the length of the observations can lead to misclassifications, no matter what their textual content is. Like with other spurious features, using this shortcut also impacts the performance of explanation mechanisms, because the main features that are exploited are not based on the textual content. Another problem is that sequence length learning gives artificial overperformance with the training and test datasets. This performance distortion leads to unfair comparisons for model selection, because some models may converge to a local minimum that uses sequence length instead of fully representing the textual information. So overall sequence length should be avoided, because the performance gain comes at the expense of model robustness, explainability and evaluation.

- motivation: seldom in public/open datasets, but we hit it in our work (early warnings of catastrophic (costly) claims for analysts); basic vs catastrophic claim files have different length profiles
- contributions: (1) empirical study of how transformer-based models are affected by sequence length learning; (2) evaluation of techniques using pretrained transformers to mitigate it
- organization: Section 2 literature; Section 3 experiments with four textual classification datasets; Section 4 data-centric mitigation techniques

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based models are the current go-to models for state-of-the-art performance, and they get impressive performances in most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. These models have a lot of parameters and are trained on huge corpora, so they retain most of the information in the training data, and this leads to significant improvements. But sometimes these improvements rely on correlations in the training and test data that are unknown and undesirable. Models can learn to use these correlations as classification shortcuts.

Bias is a well-known source of shortcuts. For example, a model that uses bias as a shortcut could associate gender and occupation together instead of learning useful textual representations that would help it infer the occupation of someone. Using shortcuts can make the model better during construction, since the models are good for the wrong reasons, but it can create problems along the value chain when the end users do not know what heuristic is used. Spurious features are another source of classification shortcuts. In this case the inductive model bias is generated by artifacts from the annotation process or from the text structure, so the models learn the dataset and not the task.

A shortcut that is less known is the difference in sequence length between observations of different classes in a classification task. If a model exploits this feature, then any variation in the length of the observations can lead to misclassifications, no matter what their textual content is. Like with other spurious features, using this shortcut also impacts the performance of explanation mechanisms, because the main features that are exploited are not based on the textual content. Another problem is that sequence length learning gives artificial overperformance with the training and test datasets. This performance distortion leads to unfair comparisons for model selection, because some models may converge to a local minimum that uses sequence length instead of fully representing the textual information. So overall sequence length should be avoided, because the performance gain comes at the expense of model robustness, explainability and evaluation.

This problem is seldom encountered in public and open datasets, but we encounter it in our work, where we want to provide analysts with early warnings of catastrophic (costly) claims. Basic claim files and catastrophic claim files have different length profiles, so sequence length learning hampers our modeling efforts.

In this paper we present two contributions related to this problem. The first one is an empirical study of how sequence length learning affects transformer-based models. The second one is an evaluation of techniques that use the capabilities of pretrained transformers to mitigate the impacts of this feature.

The rest of the paper goes as follows. In Section 2 we describe how the literature identifies and addresses the problem. In Section 3 we present a series of experiments on the impact of the sequence length meta-feature using four textual classification datasets. Finally, in Section 4 we analyze data-centric techniques to mitigate the impact of learning sequence length meta-features.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformer-based models [1], the current go-to models for state-of-the-art performance, achieve impressive performances in most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Being parameter-heavy models trained on huge corpora, they retain most of the information of the training data [2], which leads to significant improvements. However, these improvements sometimes rely on unknown and undesirable correlations present in the training and test data. Models can learn to leverage these correlations as classification shortcuts [3].

A well-known source of shortcuts is bias. Using bias as a shortcut, a model could, for instance, associate gender and occupation together [4] instead of learning useful textual representations that would help infer someone's occupation. Even though shortcuts can lead to model improvements during construction since they are good for the wrong reasons [5], they can create problems along the value chain if end users are not aware of the heuristic being used. Other sources of classification shortcut include spurious features, where inductive model bias is generated by artifacts from the annotation process or text structure, so models learn the dataset instead of the task.

A lesser-known classification shortcut is the difference in sequence length between observations of different classes in a classification task. Exploiting this feature means that any variation in the length of observations, regardless of their textual content, can lead to misclassifications. As with other spurious features, using this shortcut also impacts the performance of explanation mechanisms, since the main features exploited are not based on textual content. Another problem with sequence length learning is artificial overperformance on the training and test datasets. Such a performance distortion leads to unfair comparisons for model selection, since some models may converge to a local minimum using sequence length rather than fully representing the textual information. Overall, sequence length should be avoided because the performance gain comes at the expense of model robustness, explainability, and evaluation.

Although this problem is seldom encountered in public and open datasets, we encounter it in our work, where we aim to provide analysts with early warnings of catastrophic (costly) claims. Since basic and catastrophic claim files have different length profiles, our modeling efforts are hampered by sequence length learning.

This paper presents two contributions related to the problem described above. Our first contribution is an empirical study of how transformer-based models are affected by sequence length learning. Our second contribution is an evaluation of techniques using the capabilities of pretrained transformers to mitigate the impacts of this feature.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes how the literature identifies and addresses the problem. In Section 3, we present a series of experiments investigating the impact of the sequence length meta-feature on four textual classification datasets. Finally, in Section 4 we analyze data-centric techniques to mitigate the impact of learning sequence length meta-features.
